plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 16: Chemistry of Benzene: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a reaction energy diagram set inside a pale blue rectangular panel, following benzene and bromine along two competing pathways. A tall arrow at the far left, shaded from pale yellow at the bottom to orange at the top, is labeled "Energy"; the horizontal axis beneath the panel reads "Reaction progress" and ends in a magenta arrow. Reactants sit on a dashed level at the left, drawn as a benzene hexagon, a plus sign, and "Br2" in magenta. A black curve climbs from that level to a high first maximum capped by a short dashed line, with a vertical double-headed arrow between maximum and reactant level labeled delta-G double-dagger. The curve drops into a trough, where a cationic intermediate is drawn as a partly unsaturated six-membered ring bearing an H and a magenta Br on the same carbon with a plus sign above it, then rises to a lower second maximum and falls to a dashed product level below the reactants, where bromobenzene plus "HBr" sit above the word "Substitution"; a small double-headed arrow labeled delta-G degrees spans the reactant-to-product gap. From the same trough a magenta curve branches upward over its own maximum and ends above the reactant level at a bracketed dibrominated ring labeled "Addition" and "(does not occur)". Placing both endpoints on one vertical energy scale is what carries the argument: the substitution branch finishes downhill while the addition branch finishes uphill.

interactionPlan.concept: Electrophilic bromination of benzene passes through two activation barriers and a cationic arenium intermediate, and the substitution branch is observed (while addition is not) because substitution ends downhill in free energy whereas addition ends uphill.

interactions.label: Step along substitution path
interactions.teaches: Stepping through the black curve shows the reaction climbing a first barrier to a cationic arenium intermediate, then a second smaller barrier, before falling to substitution products — i.e. two distinct activation barriers bracket one shared intermediate

interactions.label: Pathway
interactions.teaches: Both branches share the same first barrier and arenium intermediate, but the substitution branch finishes below the reactant level (downhill, occurs) while the addition branch finishes above it (uphill, does not occur) — the relative endpoint energy decides which pathway is observed

Clicking the tall arrow emphasizes ΔG‡ (reactant level to first peak = activation energy, a kinetic barrier), while clicking the short arrow emphasizes ΔG° (reactant level to product level = overall reaction free energy, a thermodynamic driving force); the two measure different vertical gaps on the same energy scale

demo_steps.title: Reactants on the energy scale
demo_steps.narration: Benzene and Br2 sit on the dashed reactant level at the left of a single vertical energy scale; everything that follows is read as a height on this scale.

demo_steps.title: Two barriers, one intermediate
demo_steps.narration: Step the black curve forward: it climbs the tall first barrier (ΔG‡) into the cationic arenium intermediate in the trough, then a second smaller barrier, before dropping to products — substitution is a two-step, two-barrier process.

demo_steps.title: Substitution ends downhill
demo_steps.narration: At the products stage the bromobenzene + HBr level lies below the reactants, so ΔG° is negative and the substitution branch is thermodynamically favored.

demo_steps.title: Why addition does not occur
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the magenta addition branch: it leaves the same intermediate but climbs to a dibrominated product that sits above the reactant level — an uphill endpoint, which is why this pathway does not occur.

demo_steps.title: Activation energy vs overall free energy
demo_steps.narration: Click the tall arrow to highlight ΔG‡ (kinetic barrier to the first peak) and the short arrow to highlight ΔG° (thermodynamic gap to the products); they are different vertical distances on the same scale and answer different questions.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Substitution and addition share the same first barrier and arenium intermediate, so the deciding factor is the final step's thermodynamics: substitution ends below the reactant level (downhill, occurs) while addition ends above it (uphill, does not occur).
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Lay out a pale blue panel with a left-edge vertical gradient arrow (pale yellow bottom to orange top) labeled 'Energy' and a bottom 'Reaction progress' label ending in a magenta arrow. Draw the black substitution curve as a smooth two-hump profile: tall first peak (dashed cap), deep trough, lower second peak, then a steep fall to a dashed product level clearly below the dashed reactant level. Place the benzene + magenta 'Br2' at the reactant level, the arenium cation (ring with H and magenta Br on one carbon, '+' above) in the trough, and bromobenzene + 'HBr' over the word 'Substitution' at the product level. From the same trough draw a magenta curve rising over its own maximum to a bracketed dibrominated ring above the reactant level, labeled 'Addition' with magenta '(does not occur)'. Add the vertical double-headed 'ΔG‡' arrow between the first peak and reactant level and the small 'ΔG°' double-headed arrow across the reactant-product gap. Use black for the substitution curve and magenta for the addition curve and all Br-related text so the two branches and the bromine atoms read consistently; keep both endpoint levels on one shared vertical scale since that comparison is the entire argument.

authoredContext:
Why does the reaction of Br2 with benzene take a different course than its reaction with an alkene? The answer is straightforward. If addition occurred, the 150 kJ/mol stabilization energy of the aromatic ring would be lost and the overall reaction would be endergonic. When substitution occurs, though, the stability of the aromatic ring is retained and the reaction is exergonic. An energy diagram for the overall process is shown in the figure.

An energy diagram for the electrophilic bromination of benzene. Because the stability of the aromatic ring is retained, the overall process is exergonic.

Energy diagram shows curve exhibiting two peaks, with the first peak higher than second. A second curve originates from the trough of the first curve and ends higher in energy than the first curve.
